title: When does rotor cant pay on a small quadrotor co-designed with its motors and controller?
lede: research programme: fixed rotor cant on a co-designed quadrotor; with roll, pitch and yaw sharing one thrust polytope through an attitude-priority mixer, cant cuts attitude error by 6.1° (5 of 5 seeds), and pricing hover power shrinks the vehicle 5× but leaves the chosen cant at 28–37°
summary: An open research programme (target IEEE RA-L) on when a fixed rotor cant angle pays on a small quadrotor once arm, propeller, motor headroom and attitude controller are designed with it. Milestone 1 found that the torque limits of seven earlier simulated steps understated yaw authority by 2× to 2.8×; cant still beat no cant by 4.8° RMS. Milestone 2 makes roll, pitch and yaw share one thrust polytope through an attitude-priority mixer (as PX4 and Betaflight do) and puts a price on hover power. Without cant the tuned vehicle saturates roll and pitch on 97% of steps and yaw gets nothing; cant's paired advantage grows to 6.08° (SD 0.28, 5 of 5 seeds). Pricing power at 0.3° per 100 W cuts hover power 4–7× for under 0.5° of error, but the chosen cant stays at 28–37° in 9 of 10 seed-arms (best of three CMA-ES starts), refuting the hypothesis of a small 5–20° optimum; cant still wins the priced objective in 5 of 5 seeds at 0.3 and 4 of 5 at 1° per 100 W. Single-start CMA-ES is unreliable on the polytope (2 of 5 seeds fell to low cant). Simulated; TWR fixed at 2; the power price is a swept modelling choice; mass, cost and motor fits and plant ranges are inherited assumptions; no hardware.
